# Is there a scientific method? {#sec-session-01}

**Meeting 1 of 13**

[Drafted]{.status .drafted} [v0.4 · not yet held · [record discussion](../notes.qmd)]{.status-line}

## Central question

Is hypothesis-testing a universal account of inquiry, a standard for justification, or one useful mode among several?

## Anchor and companion

- Everyone reads the selected anchor sections and the companion abstract/overview. The rotating reader presents the companion in depth.
- Pairing: Methodological ideal / evidential counterpoint. Full records and access notes: [bibliography](../bibliography.qmd).

### Anchor

Platt, J. R. (1964). Strong Inference. *Science, 146*(3642), 347–353. [https://doi.org/10.1126/science.146.3642.347](<https://doi.org/10.1126/science.146.3642.347>)

Read Platt in full. Identify the role of alternative explanations and discriminating observations.

### Companion

Cleland, C. E. (2001). Historical science, experimental science, and the scientific method. *Geology, 29*(11), 987–990. [https://doi.org/10.1130/0091-7613(2001)029%3C0987:HSESAT%3E2.0.CO;2](<https://doi.org/10.1130/0091-7613(2001)029%3C0987:HSESAT%3E2.0.CO;2>)

Read Cleland’s Geology paper in full. It makes the argument in four pages, for geologists.

## Why these readings belong together

Platt offers a prescriptive strategy; Cleland analyzes differences between experimental interventions and reconstructing past events. Neither paper directly records this group’s daily research. Test both against an actual project rather than declaring one a complete scientific method. [@platt1964; @cleland2001]

## Reading notes

[Drafted]{.status .drafted} [convenor notes written before the meeting · revise after discussion]{.status-line}

### Platt: what the paper says

- The claim is that some fields advance an order of magnitude faster than others, and that the main reason is a method rather than talent, tractability, or money. Platt names the method "strong inference": (1) devise alternative hypotheses; (2) devise a crucial experiment with alternative outcomes, each of which excludes one or more hypotheses; (3) run it for a clean result; (1′) recycle with subhypotheses. The elements are Bacon's; the difference is applying them "formally and explicitly and regularly" to every problem.
- The second ingredient is Chamberlin's method of multiple working hypotheses [@chamberlin1965], written by a geologist. Its purpose is affective as much as logical: a single hypothesis becomes the owner's "intellectual child," and multiple hypotheses "distribute the effort and divide the affections," turning conflict between people into conflict between ideas.
- The private test Platt calls "The Question" runs in both directions. On hearing a theory: what experiment could disprove it? On hearing an experiment: what hypothesis does it disprove? He proposes it as a standard for judging one's own work and, in passing, for funding decisions.
- The pathologies he lists are recognizable in any field: The Frozen Method, The Eternal Surveyor, The Never Finished, The Great Man With a Single Hypothesis, The All-Encompassing Theory Which Can Never Be Falsified. Surveys, taxonomy, instrument design, tables, and computations are honored only "as parts of a chain of precise induction"; otherwise they are bricks lying around the brickyard.
- On quantification, Platt argues that a qualitative exclusion can be more rigorous than a two-decimal fit, and that "we substitute correlations for causal studies." His image is that phenomena can be caught in a logical box, coarse but strong, or a mathematical box, fine-grained but flimsy.
- The practical aid is a notebook: a half hour a day writing out the logical tree, the alternatives, and the crucial experiments (Fermi, Faraday, the blackboards at the Laboratory of Molecular Biology).

What the paper does not establish. It is the text of a 1963 address to physical chemists, and its evidence is a set of selected successes: molecular biology, parity violation, Pasteur, Roentgen. No comparison sample is offered, so the association between method and speed is asserted rather than shown. Platt concedes that the grand syntheses of Newton and Maxwell "stand outside any rule or method," and he hands the generative step, inventing the hypotheses and the experiment, to Pólya. His yardstick is speed, "information per unit time," and he adopts Popper's disproof in a paragraph without examining it. Read the paper as a normative proposal with anecdotal support, which is how the case exercise should treat it.

### Cleland: what the paper says

- The target is the claim, made most sharply by Henry Gee, that hypotheses about the past cannot be tested by experiment and are therefore unscientific. Cleland answers in two moves.
- First move: the accounts of method behind that claim, inductivism and falsificationism, are flawed. A failed prediction never isolates the target hypothesis, because every test carries auxiliary assumptions about instruments, samples, and background theory. Modus tollens says one premise is false, not which one. When Uranus misbehaved, astronomers kept Newton and rejected the auxiliary assumption that there was no outer planet. Looking at what experimentalists do, Cleland reads their practice as holding the test condition fixed while varying auxiliary conditions, which protects the hypothesis from false negatives after a failure and from false positives after a success. That is not ruthless falsification.
- Second move: there is a real methodological difference, and it follows from a feature of nature that Lewis called the asymmetry of overdetermination. Localized present events overdetermine their causes and underdetermine their effects. A small subcollection of a volcano's ash, pumice, and gases suffices to infer the eruption, and many such subcollections would do; predicting the eruption requires knowing an open-ended set of conditions. The perfect crime is hard for the same reason.
- Historical practice therefore looks different. Historical scientists formulate multiple competing hypotheses about a particular past event and search for a smoking gun: a trace that picks out one hypothesis as the better causal explanation of the available traces. The K–T iridium and shocked quartz became a smoking gun for the impact hypothesis only once the timing of the extinction was constrained. A smoking gun may be predicted from the hypothesis (the microwave background) or stumbled on (iridium); traces attenuate with time, may need new technology to detect, and can lose their status when new rivals or evidence appear.
- Laboratory and computational work has a different role in historical science. Lab analysis sharpens traces (carbon isotopes in small grains) or tests auxiliary assumptions (Miller–Urey tested that amino acids can form, not that life began that way). A computer model determines the consequences of a hypothesis under a small number of explicitly represented conditions; it cannot say which conditions obtained, and early snowball Earth simulations omitted volcanic carbon dioxide. "Modeling past events is theoretical work."
- The obligation that follows is stated plainly: failure to search for a smoking gun deprives a historical hypothesis of empirical grounding and turns it into a just-so story. The charge is about practice, not about the kind of hypothesis.

What the paper does not establish. It is a philosophical argument with illustrative cases, not a study of what geologists do day to day. Cleland leaves open whether the asymmetry is deterministic or probabilistic. The paper addresses how hypotheses are warranted, not how they are generated, and it says little about which traces to look for first or what a search costs. The experimental/historical contrast is drawn as a dichotomy; much of our work sits between the two, and meeting 9 [@oreskes1994] returns to the model case.

### Where the two papers meet

- Both build on Chamberlin. Both prefer discrimination among rivals to confirmation of one. "The Question" and the smoking gun are two names for the same demand: does this evidence tell rivals apart?
- The unit of progress differs. Platt's unit is an intervention designed in advance so that each outcome excludes something. Cleland's unit is a trace found in nature, often not predicted, whose discriminating power may only become clear after other traces constrain the timing.
- Platt treats exclusion as the one secure conclusion. Cleland's first move shows that exclusion is never clean, since an auxiliary assumption can absorb any failure. Platt's loop needs Cleland's correction to be usable.
- Platt's brickyard and Cleland's smoking guns are in tension. The iridium anomaly came from a measurement program undertaken for another purpose (a sedimentation-rate clock, per Alvarez and colleagues' 1980 paper), and the microwave background was found by engineers testing an antenna. Some surveys are trace collection rather than time-serving, and the difference is not visible in advance.

### Relevance for Earth science research

- Most questions in this group are historical or observational in Cleland's sense: what ruptured, what structure produced these waveforms, what happened along the Cascadia margin. Interventions are rare, and the field runs on traces. Cleland supplies a defensible account of why that is not second-rate science, and names the obligation that comes with it.
- The asymmetry of overdetermination separates two activities we often discuss together. Attribution after an event exploits overdetermination, which is why a few well-chosen traces can settle a source mechanism. Forecasting sits on the underdetermined side, where an open-ended set of conditions matters. The two deserve different evidence standards, and meeting 3 [@atwater1987] is the group's first trace-based case.
- Platt's loop applies wherever we choose what to observe. A DAS or nodal deployment, a rock-deformation experiment, a synthetic test, or a new station can each be designed so that rival mechanisms predict different signals. "What hypothesis does this deployment exclude?" is a fair question for a proposal or a field plan.
- Cleland's account of experimental practice describes what we do when a result looks too good: hold the target fixed and vary the auxiliaries, which for us means the instrument response, the velocity model, the noise sources, and the processing chain. The worked example in the [agent design](../agent-design.qmd) page follows this pattern for seasonal velocity change.
- Cleland's warning about models transfers directly to numerical simulation and to machine-learned predictors. A simulation yields conditional consequences under represented conditions, and a correlation learned from a catalog is not a causal study. Platt's question, what does this model exclude, is the corrective.
- Platt's pathologies have Earth science forms: a catalog built without a question, one inversion code applied to every problem, one instrument defining a career. The group should decide, on cases, when a catalog is a brick in the brickyard and when it is trace collection that a later smoking gun will need.

### What this should translate to in agent behavior

The following are design hypotheses, drawn from the two papers and aligned with the [hypothesis](../modes/hypothesis.qmd), [synthesis](../modes/synthesis.qmd), and [exploration](../modes/exploration.qmd) profiles. None is an established policy; each is something the evaluation in meeting 13 could test.

1. Before proposing an observation, computation, or experiment, state at least two substantive rivals and what each predicts differently. Verbal variants of one idea do not count.
2. Answer The Question in both directions for every proposed action: which rival would this result exclude, and which rival would exclude it? If neither has an answer, label the action as exploration or estimation rather than dressing it as a test.
3. Treat exclusion as provisional. On a failed prediction, list the auxiliary assumptions that could absorb the failure and rank which to check first, rather than dropping the hypothesis. On a successful prediction, check for false positives by varying auxiliaries and removing the test condition.
4. For a historical question, name the smoking gun: the trace whose presence or character would favor one account. Say whether it is predicted by the hypothesis or must be found, whether it is likely preserved, what measurement it needs, and what the search would cost.
5. Separate three kinds of laboratory and computational work in the record: sharpening a trace, testing an auxiliary assumption, and testing the historical hypothesis itself. Record a simulation result as a conditional consequence with its represented conditions, never as a test outcome.
6. Keep the logical tree as an inspectable artifact: rivals, planned discriminators, outcomes, exclusions, and pruned branches, updated each cycle. Platt's daily notebook becomes the [claim record](../rubrics.qmd#claim-record) and the [episode ledger](../rubrics.qmd#inquiry-mode-ledger).
7. Permit collection, description, and survey without a rival set, but label the mode and ask Platt's yardstick periodically: what could this survey let us exclude later? Whether a rival set should be required before every action is a policy to evaluate, not a premise ([glossary](../glossary.qmd#action-commitment-and-claim-status)).
8. Rivals are not the agent's property. When every rival accommodates the evidence, return to exploration or acquire a new observable rather than defending the incumbent.
9. Prefer a qualitative exclusion to a marginal quantitative fit where the qualitative test discriminates more. Report what a fit excludes, not only its residual.

### Questions to bring to the meeting

- Is a smoking gun a crucial experiment that nature ran, or does the difference between a planned intervention and a found trace matter for how an agent should plan?
- Does Platt's yardstick of information per unit time make sense when the limiting step is trace discovery or instrument development?
- Which of the group's current projects follows Platt's loop, which is searching for a smoking gun, and which is doing neither? That is the case exercise.
- Would an agent that must state rivals before every action perform worse on exploratory tasks? Meeting 2 and meeting 6 bear on this; it should be tested rather than assumed.

## Prepare and discuss

Read the selected anchor sections and the companion abstract or overview. Bring one source passage or artifact relevant to the case; the rotating reader presents the companion in depth.

1. Can an observational study discriminate hypotheses without controlling the system?
2. Which research actions are not well described as a test?
3. Are we describing how ideas are generated or how claims are warranted?

## Case exercise: scientific gain and epistemic mode

Compare Platt and Cleland on one documented case. State a meaningful before/after scientific gain, then identify which proposed mode definition succeeds or fails on the case. Distinguish a normative argument from evidence of what scientists did.

- Profiles to examine: [hypothesis](../modes/hypothesis.qmd), [synthesis](../modes/synthesis.qmd), [exploration](../modes/exploration.qmd).
- Record source kind and unknown chronology; distinguish documented practice, philosophical argument, association, and our proposed agent rule.
- Ask what was gained, what warrants it, which action helped, and what a comparable agent would need to demonstrate.

| Minutes | Activity |
|:--|:--|
| 0–5 | Frame the scientific question and possible advance. |
| 5–15 | Companion presented by the rotating reader. |
| 15–40 | Discuss the sources and their limits. |
| 40–55 | Work through the case and its agent/evaluation implications. |
| 55–60 | Add the shared record and one unresolved question. |

## Shared output

One episode entry and three sentences: what changed scientifically; what evidence warrants that account; what agent action or evaluation follows. Longer worksheets are optional.

- [Episode ledger](../rubrics.qmd#inquiry-mode-ledger) · [Advance profile](../rubrics.qmd#scientific-advance-profile-v1) · [Claim record](../rubrics.qmd#claim-record).
- Facilitator framing: compare knowledge/understanding accounts in @dellsen2016; introduce advance now and revisit its measurement in meeting 12.

## Optional extensions

- @chamberlin1965: [The Method of Multiple Working Hypotheses](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.148.3671.754). Science (1965). Written by a geologist, and the source Platt built on. Chamberlin's target is the single ruling hypothesis; his remedy is to hold a family of them at once. Decide whether Platt's loop and Chamberlin's family are the same practice.
- @simon1973: [Does Scientific Discovery Have a Logic?](https://doi.org/10.1086/288559). Philosophy of Science (1973). Simon argues, against Popper, that discovery is problem solving with describable heuristics. The computer discovery programs listed in [meeting 13](13-agent-design-and-evaluation.qmd) were built on this argument.
- @klahr1988: [Dual Space Search During Scientific Reasoning](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog1201_1). Cognitive Science (1988). People solving a discovery task searched two spaces, one of hypotheses and one of experiments, and some made progress by running experiments with no hypothesis at all. Experimental evidence that inquiry has more than one search mode.
- @holmes1987: [Scientific Writing and Scientific Discovery](https://doi.org/10.1086/354391). Isis (1987). Holmes compared laboratory notebooks with the published papers written from them and describes what the paper leaves out. The basis for standing question 5.
- @gilbert1896: [The Origin of Hypotheses, Illustrated by the Discussion of a Topographic Problem](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.3.53.1). Science (1896). Grove Karl Gilbert on where a geological hypothesis comes from, worked through his own attempt to explain the Coon Butte crater: by analogy, by enumeration of the possible causes, and by the test that separates them. The geological ancestor of Platt's method, and an account of the generative step Platt hands to Pólya.
- @johnson1933: [Role of Analysis in Scientific Investigation](https://doi.org/10.1130/GSAB-44-461). Geological Society of America Bulletin (1933). A geologist's account of analysis as the method of geological investigation, with the failure modes it guards against.
- @frodeman1995: [Geological reasoning: Geology as an interpretive and historical science](https://doi.org/10.1130/0016-7606(1995)107%3C0960:GRGAAI%3E2.3.CO;2). Geological Society of America Bulletin (1995). Geology as an interpretive and historical science, against the physics model of method. The geological statement of Cleland's thesis, seven years earlier.
- @kleinhans2005: [Terra Incognita: Explanation and Reduction in Earth Science](https://doi.org/10.1080/02698590500462356). International Studies in the Philosophy of Science (2005). What explanation and reduction mean in earth science, where the systems are open and the histories unique.
- @elliott2007: [Revisiting Chamberlin: Multiple Working Hypotheses for the 21st Century](https://doi.org/10.1641/B570708). BioScience (2007). Chamberlin's multiple working hypotheses reconsidered for present-day practice, with the model-selection tools that now implement them.
- @cleland2002: [Methodological and Epistemic Differences between Historical Science and Experimental Science](https://doi.org/10.1086/342455). Longer development of experimental/historical differences; optional elaboration of the companion.
- @hacking1992: [‘Style’ for historians and philosophers](https://doi.org/10.1016/0039-3681(92)90024-z). Historical/philosophical framing for plural styles; these precedents do not validate our profiles.
- @fortunato2018: [Science of science](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aao0185). A broad science-of-science orientation; distinguish process, population associations, and impact measures.
- @dellsen2016: [Scientific progress: Knowledge versus understanding](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.shpsa.2016.01.003). An understanding-based account of progress to compare with knowledge and capability gains.
